---
title: Does Money Buy Wins? An Analysis of Payroll Efficiency in Major League Baseball
  (2021–2026)
author: "Borna Anic-Matic"
date: "2026-10-30"
output:
  html_document: default
  pdf_document: default
---

As the 2026 MLB season comes to an end, with the Milwaukee Brewers crowned World Series champions for the first time in franchise history, discussions surrounding a potential lockout and the introduction of salary caps and floors have raised an important question: **To what extent does a team's payroll predict its success?**

This project aims to investigate the relationship between team payroll and regular-season success in Major League Baseball from 2021 to 2026, examining whether payroll can serve as a reliable predictor of a team's performance.

```{r}
install.packages('baseballr')
install.packages("rvest")
install.packages("readxl")

```
```{r}
library(baseballr)
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(readxl)



```

```{r}

# Create an empty list to store standings
standings_list <- list()

# Loop through each year
for (year in 2021:2026) {

  # Retrieve American League standings
  AL <- mlb_standings(
    season = year,
    league_id = 103
  )

  # Retrieve National League standings
  NL <- mlb_standings(
    season = year,
    league_id = 104
  )

  # Combine both leagues
  season_standings <- bind_rows(AL, NL)

  # Add the year as a variable
  season_standings$year <- year

  # Store the results
  standings_list[[as.character(year)]] <- season_standings
}

# Combine all seasons into one dataframe
mlb_standings_all <- bind_rows(standings_list)
```


```{r}
excel_sheets("MLB Salaries.xlsx")

payroll_data <- bind_rows(
  lapply(2021:2026, function(year) {
    read_excel(
      "MLB Salaries.xlsx",
      sheet = as.character(year)
    )
  })
)
```
```{r}
#View(payroll_data)

dim(payroll_data)

names(payroll_data)
```

```{r}
mlb_payroll <- payroll_data %>% 
               mutate(`difference in payroll` = `team payroll` - `last year payroll`)  %>%
               select(year, team, `team payroll`, w, l, `last year payroll`, `difference in payroll`) 

mlb_payroll

```
```{r}
summary(mlb_payroll)
```

## Examining the Relationship Between Team Payroll and Regular-Season Performance (2021–2026)

To begin the anyalsis, we will be comparing a teams payroll for a given year versue the amount of wins and losses they obtained. To do this we will first graph the data agaisnt each other and then we will calculate correaltion tests to quantify what the graphs are showing.
```{r}
# Payroll vs Wins
ggplot(mlb_payroll, aes(x = `team payroll`, y = w)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(
      scale = 1e-6,
      prefix = "$",
      suffix = "M"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Team Payroll vs Regular-Season Wins (2021–2026)",
    x = "Team Payroll",
    y = "Wins"
  )

# Payroll vs Losses
ggplot(mlb_payroll, aes(x = `team payroll`, y = l)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(
      scale = 1e-6,
      prefix = "$",
      suffix = "M"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Team Payroll vs Regular-Season Losses (2021–2026)",
    x = "Team Payroll",
    y = "Losses"
  )
```
```{r}
cor_win_payroll <- cor(mlb_payroll$w,mlb_payroll$`team payroll`)
cor_loss_payroll <- cor(mlb_payroll$l,mlb_payroll$`team payroll`)

rsqu_win_payroll <- cor(mlb_payroll$w,mlb_payroll$`team payroll`)^2
rsqu_loss_payroll <- cor(mlb_payroll$l,mlb_payroll$`team payroll`)^2

cor_win_payroll
cor_loss_payroll
rsqu_win_payroll
rsqu_loss_payroll
```

The relationship between team payroll and wins appears to be positively correlated, although the strength of this relationship is relatively weak to moderate. An R-squared value of 0.1167 indicates that approximately 11.67% of the variation in a team's wins can be explained by its payroll.

Conversely, the relationship between team payroll and losses is negative, with a similarly weak to moderate correlation. An R-squared value of 0.1177 indicates that approximately 11.77% of the variation in a team's losses can be explained by its payroll.

Overall, these findings suggest that team payroll alone is a relatively weak predictor of regular-season performance. While higher payrolls are generally associated with more wins and fewer losses, a substantial proportion of the variation in team performance remains unexplained by payroll alone.

## Examining the Relationship Between Year-Over-Year Changes in Team Payroll and Regular-Season Performance (2021–2026)

```{r}
payroll_data_2 <- payroll_data %>% group_by(team) %>%
                  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
                  mutate(wins_change = w - lag(w)) %>%
                  ungroup()

payroll_data_2 <- payroll_data_2 %>% group_by(team) %>%
                  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
                  mutate(losses_change = l - lag(l)) %>%
                  ungroup()

payroll_data_2 <- payroll_data_2 %>% group_by(team) %>%
                  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
                  mutate(payroll_change = `team payroll` - lag(`team payroll`)) %>%
                  ungroup()
```

```{r}
payroll_data_2 <- payroll_data_2 %>%
  tidyr::drop_na(wins_change, losses_change, payroll_change)
```

```{r}
avg_win_change <-mean(payroll_data_2$wins_change)
avg_win_change

avg_loss_change <- mean(payroll_data_2$losses_change)
avg_loss_change

avg_payroll_change <- mean(payroll_data_2$payroll_change)
avg_payroll_change
```

```{r}
# Change in Payroll vs Change in Wins
ggplot(payroll_data_2, aes(x = payroll_change, y = wins_change)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(
      scale = 1e-6,
      prefix = "$",
      suffix = "M"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Team Payroll Change vs Regular-Season Wins Change",
    x = "Team Payroll Change",
    y = "Wins Change"
  )

ggplot(payroll_data_2, aes(x = payroll_change, y = losses_change)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(
      scale = 1e-6,
      prefix = "$",
      suffix = "M"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Team Payroll Change vs Regular-Season Losses Change",
    x = "Team Payroll Change",
    y = "Losses Change"
  )
```
```{r}
cor_winschange_payrollchange <- cor(payroll_data_2$wins_change, payroll_data_2$payroll_change)
cor_losseschange_payrollchange <-cor(payroll_data_2$losses_change, payroll_data_2$payroll_change)

cor_winschange_payrollchange
cor_losseschange_payrollchange

cor_winschange_payrollchange^2
cor_losseschange_payrollchange^2
```
The relationship between year-over-year changes in team payroll and changes in regular-season performance appears to be extremely weak.

The correlation between changes in payroll and wins was -0.0759, indicating a very weak negative relationship. An R-squared value of 0.00576 suggests that approximately 0.58% of the variation in year-over-year changes in wins can be explained by changes in team payroll.

Conversely, the correlation between changes in payroll and losses was 0.0781, indicating a very weak positive relationship. The corresponding R-squared value of 0.00611 indicates that approximately 0.61% of the variation in changes in losses can be explained by changes in payroll.

Overall, these findings suggest that increases or decreases in team payroll have little linear association with improvements or declines in regular-season performance. While changes in spending may influence individual teams, the results indicate that payroll changes alone are not reliable predictors of year-over-year changes in wins or losses across Major League Baseball.
